claims.text: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 has a single-phase FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy has high dislocation density and refined grains.
The as-built alloy has process-induced compositional inhomogeneities at grain boundaries.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by selective, diffusion-controlled oxidation of Al and Ti at grain boundaries and residual-defect aggregates.
Under reducing conditions, reactive elements undergo a non-protective reduction process at high-energy sites.
Grain boundaries and defect sites act as fast diffusion pathways for Al and Ti.
Oxidizing exposure produces a thin, discontinuous alumina/titania-based scale along high-energy grain-boundary networks.
Residual stresses and compositional fluctuations prevent formation of a uniform, adherent protective oxide layer.
Reducing exposure promotes internal void formation or inadequate passivation in high-diffusivity regions.
Brittle reaction layers compromise intergranular cohesion.
Compromised intergranular cohesion and residual stress cause rapid microcrack coalescence and catastrophic failure.
Oxidizing exposure will produce localized continuous oxide layers along grain boundaries with associated microcracks.
Reducing exposure will produce internal voids or less-protective interfacial films.
Both oxidizing and reducing exposures will significantly reduce fracture toughness or tensile ductility relative to the as-built state.
Catastrophic failure will be preceded by observable intergranular damage.
The as-built baseline is compositionally homogeneous and has minimal oxidation or microcracking.
The proposed grain-boundary reaction mechanism dominates at 850–950 °C when the gas has sufficient oxidizing or reducing potential.
Degradation should be minimal below 850 °C or under inert atmospheres.
Al depletion should occur near oxidized or otherwise degraded regions.
Subtle phase transformations associated with processing or exposure may alter the rate and extent of degradation.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field asserts process-induced compositional inhomogeneities at grain boundaries, whereas the baseline describes the as-built microstructure as homogeneous.
The hypothesis and mechanism predict a discontinuous oxide layer, but the predicted outcome calls for localized continuous oxide layers along grain boundaries.
